name: Technology Bubble Dynamics
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: How Real Money Chases an Unproven Curve
lesson.summary: When capital markets price in an optimistic future as if it were already the present, the resulting financial bubble tracks the hype cycle's peak closely, but a bubble bursting is a verdict on pricing, not necessarily on the underlying technology.
lesson.body:
A technology bubble is a period where investment, valuations, and capital formation around a technology rise well beyond what current or plausible near term fundamentals justify, driven by expectations of future value rather than present cash flow or proven capability. It typically overlaps closely with the Peak of Inflated Expectations phase of the hype cycle, but adds a specifically financial dimension, capital markets, valuations, and public offerings, that the hype cycle model does not itself track in detail.

The mechanism connects directly to the base rate established earlier: because most heavily hyped technologies underperform their promises, a bubble is essentially a market temporarily pricing in an optimistic tail outcome as though it were the expected outcome. This works for a while because early investors who get in and out before the correction can profit regardless of the technology's true long run value, which creates an incentive to keep the story going rather than to price it accurately. That loop, where rising prices themselves become evidence used to justify further rises, is sometimes called reflexivity.

The dot-com bubble of the late 1990s is a well documented example. Internet related company valuations rose to levels implying dominant, profitable market positions for companies that in many cases had no clear path to profitability, based on extrapolating early user growth rates rather than proven business models. The NASDAQ composite roughly quintupled between 1995 and its March 2000 peak, then lost most of its value by late 2002, a genuinely bubble shaped pattern in the financial data, coinciding closely with the internet's own peak of inflated expectations in public discourse.

A financial bubble popping does not mean the underlying technology was worthless, only that its financial pricing had become disconnected from near term fundamentals. The dot-com crash destroyed enormous paper wealth and many companies, but it also left behind real infrastructure, notably large amounts of fiber optic cable laid by telecommunications companies during the boom, much of which sat underused for years before later internet growth put it to productive use. A technology's long run trajectory and its bubble's financial trajectory are related but genuinely separate things.

This is the crucial distinction for evaluating any sector currently attracting heavy venture and public market capital: a bubble bursting is evidence about capital allocation and expectation setting, not direct evidence about the underlying science or engineering. Assuming a funding crash proves a technology was fake, or assuming heavy funding proves a technology works, are both base rate violating errors, just pointed in opposite directions.

Applied cautiously to quantum computing: the sector has drawn substantial venture investment and seen several companies go public in the 2020s, alongside sizable corporate research budgets from major technology companies, patterns that are consistent with bubble adjacent dynamics without by themselves proving a bubble exists or has burst. Reading the funding headlines as a verdict either way is a mistake. Separating the financial story from the engineering story, using the tools built up across this chapter and the ones before it, is the more useful move.
